title: Un secret au bar  (A Secret at the Bar)

segments.t: At a Parisian bar after work, Camille, Herve, and Sofia relax over drinks. The conversation turns playful until Herve blabs a huge agency secret about Camille's parentage. Let's listen to the scene in French first.
Santé à tout le monde!
Comment tu vas ce soir, Camille?
Ça va très bien, merci beaucoup.
Pourquoi tu ne sors pas avec Hippolyte?
Ne dis pas n'importe quoi, Sofia.
On est amis, c'est tout.
Tu plaisantes? Vous êtes faits l'un pour l'autre!
Non, on se ressemble trop.
Non, je vais juste aux toilettes.
Leurs pères se connaissent très bien.
Pourquoi elle ne le dit pas?
C'est un grand secret de famille.
Qui est son vrai père?
Christophe Lambert! C'est son père!
Sérieux? C'est incroyable!
Elle lui ressemble beaucoup, tu trouves aussi?
Let's explore the conversation line by line and unpack the French phrases.
Santé à tout le monde!
'Cheers to everyone!' Hervé raises his glass to toast using a handy word meaning 'health'. The French use this structure often.
Comment tu vas ce soir, Camille?
'How are you doing tonight, Camille?' Sofia checks in using the casual 'you'. In French, this phrasing is common.
Ça va très bien, merci beaucoup.
'I am doing very well, thank you very much.' Camille replies politely using an everyday expression meaning 'it goes very well'. You will find this useful in French.
Pourquoi tu ne sors pas avec Hippolyte?
'Why don't you go out with Hippolyte?' Sofia innocently asks using an action meaning 'go out' paired with a connector for 'with'. This sounds extremely natural in French.
Ne dis pas n'importe quoi, Sofia.
'Do not say foolish things, Sofia.' Camille deflects the awkward question using a handy chunk meaning 'anything'. In French, this is perfectly fine.
On est amis, c'est tout.
'We are friends, that is all.' Camille firmly sets the record straight using a direct cognate meaning 'friends'. A standard way to speak in French.
Tu plaisantes? Vous êtes faits l'un pour l'autre!
'Are you kidding? You are made for each other!' Hervé teases them enthusiastically using the formal 'you' to refer to them both. In French, you will hear this.
Non, on se ressemble trop.
'No, we are too similar.' Camille explains her hesitation using a reflexive action meaning 'we resemble each other'. The French say this often.
Non, je vais juste aux toilettes.
'No, I am just going to the restroom.' Camille excuses herself using an action meaning 'go' paired with 'to the toilets'. In French, this is quite common.
Leurs pères se connaissent très bien.
'Their fathers know each other very well.' Hervé drops a hint using a reflexive action meaning 'know each other'. This is how you say it in French.
Pourquoi elle ne le dit pas?
'Why does she not say it?' Sofia wonders why the connection is kept quiet using the action meaning 'say'. A handy phrase in French.
C'est un grand secret de famille.
'It is a big family secret.' Hervé explains the mystery using a direct cognate meaning 'secret'. A useful expression in French.
Qui est son vrai père?
'Who is her real father?' Sofia asks with curiosity using a handy question word meaning 'who'. This is very typical in French.
Christophe Lambert! C'est son père!
'Christophe Lambert! That is her father!' Hervé dramatically reveals the name of the famous actor. A common chunk in French.
Sérieux? C'est incroyable!
'Seriously? That is incredible!' Sofia reacts with astonishment using an everyday term meaning 'serious'. You will hear this in French.
Elle lui ressemble beaucoup, tu trouves aussi?

'She looks a lot like him, do you think so too?' Hervé seeks agreement using an action meaning 'resembles'. This is perfectly natural in French. Now let's listen to the entire dialogue once more to lock in what you have learned.

Herve shares the outrageous agency rumor about Camille's parentage, while Sofia reacts with total surprise. Camille's cover story remains intact for now. See you next time!
